passages.original: Sapientis quisquis abstulerit divitias, omnia illi sua relinquet ; vivit enim praesentibus laetus, futuri securus. " Nihil magis," inquit ille Socrates, aut aliquis alius, ius cui idem adversus humana atque eadem potestas est, " persuasi mihi, quam ne ad opiniones vestras actum vitae meae flecterem. Solita conferte undique verba ; non conviciari vos putabo sed vagire velut infantes miserrimos."
passages.english: Whoever takes away a wise man's riches will leave him all that is his own; for he lives glad in the present and untroubled about the future. "I have persuaded myself of nothing more firmly," says that Socrates, or some other man who has the same right and the same power over human affairs, "than that I should not bend the conduct of my life to your opinions. Gather your usual words from every side; I shall not think that you are reviling me, but that you are wailing like the most wretched infants."
passages.notes: "ius cui idem adversus humana atque eadem potestas est": literally "to whom there is the same right and the same power against human things," i.e. someone with the same authority and power to stand against human affairs (such as fortune and men's opinions). "vagire" is the crying or squalling of infants.
